# Testing and Continuous Integration {#sec-testing}

Your script reads a length-of-stay column from an institutional
warehouse, and one quarter the warehouse begins reporting it in
seconds where it previously reported days. Nothing errors. The
column is still numeric, the join still succeeds, the model still
fits, and every downstream number is wrong by a factor of 86,400.
No amount of rereading your code will find the problem, because
your code is not what changed. A one-line test asserting that
length of stay falls in a plausible range fails on the first run
after the change; this chapter is about writing that line, about
finding out whether the tests you already have would notice
anything at all, and about running them, through continuous
integration, on a clean machine every time the code changes.

::: {.bookepigraph}
```{=latex}
\begin{flushright}\small
```
*Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs,
but never to show their absence.*

[Edsger W. Dijkstra]{.smallcaps}, *Notes on Structured
Programming* (1970)
```{=latex}
\end{flushright}
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: testing-pipeline-setup
#| include: false
source('_pipeline.R')
```

#| echo: false

#| fig-alt: !expr pipeline_alt('analyze')
pipeline_diagram('analyze')

## Why test an analysis {#sec-testing-why}

Analysis code rarely gets tested, and the reason is a respectable
one. Software is written to run on inputs its author has never
seen; an analysis script is written to run on one dataset, once.
The reasoning has two holes. The script does not run once: it runs
every time an extract is refreshed, an exclusion is revised, or a
reviewer asks for a sensitivity analysis, and by then its author
has forgotten which branches were ever exercised. And the failures
that matter in analysis code do not stop it running. A filter that
removes the wrong rows, a join that duplicates a patient, a unit
conversion applied twice: all produce output. The question a test
answers is not 'did it run' but 'would I have noticed if it were
wrong', and for most analysis scripts the honest answer is no.

Three ordinary occasions make the case concrete
(@tbl-testing-occasions).

| Occasion | What changes | What the test asserts |
|---|---|---|
| Refactoring | Your code, on purpose: `base::merge()` becomes a `dplyr` join | The output is identical to a saved baseline |
| Upstream drift | The data, silently: days become seconds | Values fall in plausible ranges; codes are in the codebook |
| Documentation | Nobody's memory of the intent | Given input X, the function returns Y, and a false claim fails the build |

: Three occasions a test pays for itself. {#tbl-testing-occasions}

Tests come in layers that catch different failures
(@fig-test-layers). For analysis code the pyramid familiar from
software engineering is flatter: the integration layer, a small
synthetic dataset run through the whole pipeline, does more work
here than in most applications.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-test-layers
%%| fig-alt: "Three stacked layers in increasing scope. Unit tests
%%|   exercise one function on known input, catch helper bugs, and
%%|   cost seconds. Integration tests run the whole pipeline on a
%%|   twenty-line synthetic dataset, catch composition bugs and
%%|   silent filter and join errors, and cost seconds. End-to-end
%%|   tests run raw data through to final figures, catch everything
%%|   remaining, and cost minutes to hours."
%%| fig-cap: "The three test layers and what each one catches.
%%|   Unit tests are fast and narrow; end-to-end tests are slow and
%%|   broad; the integration layer, where a synthetic dataset is run
%%|   through the whole cleaning pipeline, has the best cost-benefit
%%|   ratio for analysis code and is the layer most often missing."
flowchart TD
  U["<b>Unit</b><br/><i>one function, known input</i><br/>catches: helper bugs<br/>cost: seconds"]
  I["<b>Integration</b><br/><i>whole pipeline, 20-line<br/>synthetic dataset</i><br/>catches: composition bugs,<br/>silent filter and join errors<br/>cost: seconds"]
  E["<b>End to end</b><br/><i>raw data to final figures</i><br/>catches: everything left<br/>cost: minutes to hours"]
  U --> I --> E
```

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A cleaning script filters to adults with
`filter(age >= 18)`. Six months later someone discovers that the
export encodes unknown age as `-1`, so those rows were silently
dropped as minors. Which layer would have caught it, and what would
the test have asserted?

**Answer.** The integration layer, and only if the synthetic
dataset contained a `-1`. A unit test of the filter passes: given
ages 17, 25, and 40 it correctly keeps two. The function is not
broken; the *data* violated an assumption the function never
stated. Two assertions are worth writing, and they fail at
different times. One on the input, that `age` falls in a plausible
range before the filter runs, fails the day the export changes.
One on the output, that the number of rows dropped is what the
codebook predicts, fails the day the meaning changes. The first is
a claim about the data; the second is a claim about your
understanding of it.
:::

## Unit tests with tinytest {#sec-testing-unit}

The book uses `tinytest`. It has no dependencies of its own, which
matters when the surrounding chapters are about pinning an
environment; each test file runs on its own; and its assertion
vocabulary is small enough to hold in your head. If you will work
in a `testthat` project, @sec-testing-testthat translates.

For a function in `R/clean.R`:

```{r}
#| label: test-age-group-fn
#' Compute age groups from numeric age
#' @param age numeric vector
age_group <- function(age) {
  cut(age,
      breaks = c(0, 18, 40, 65, Inf),
      right = FALSE,
      labels = c("under-18", "18-39", "40-64", "65+"))
}
```

Tests in `inst/tinytest/test-clean.R`:

```{r}
#| label: test-age-group-tests
#| message: false
library(tinytest)

expect_equal(as.character(age_group(c(20, 50, 75))),
             c("18-39", "40-64", "65+"),
             info = "typical adult ages bin correctly")

# the interval starts are inclusive, because right = FALSE
expect_equal(as.character(age_group(c(18, 40, 65))),
             c("18-39", "40-64", "65+"),
             info = "boundary values fall in the upper bin")
expect_equal(as.character(age_group(c(17, 39, 64))),
             c("under-18", "18-39", "40-64"),
             info = "values just below a break stay below")

# NA_real_, not NA: bare NA is logical, and cut() rejects it. The
# distinction is invisible until the test is actually run.
expect_true(is.na(age_group(NA_real_)),
            info = "numeric NA propagates rather than erroring")

expect_error(age_group("twenty"),
             info = "non-numeric input is rejected")
```

Each `expect_*()` call is one test, and its `info=` string says
what it checks; a failure reports the file and line beside it. The
tests above follow the rule that edge cases are where bugs live:
boundaries, missing values, and the wrong type. For other
functions the list includes empty input, a single observation, a
group with one member, zero variance, and perfect collinearity.

Run every test file from the project root, or a package's tests
by name (display-only; both need a project with an
`inst/tinytest/` directory):

```r
tinytest::test_all()
tinytest::test_package("practicum")
```

`tinytest` expects the test files in `inst/tinytest/` and a
one-line `tests/tinytest.R` that runs them, which is the layout
`tinytest::setup_tinytest()` creates and the one `zzcollab`
scaffolds. Tests under `inst/` are installed with the package, so
someone who has your compendium can run its tests without your
source tree. For an analysis whose credibility rests on being
checkable by someone else, that is the right default.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Written as `expect_true(is.na(age_group(NA)))`, the
`NA` test errors instead of passing. What does that tell you about
the function, beyond the test?

**Answer.** Bare `NA` is logical, and `cut()` requires a numeric
argument, so `age_group(NA)` stops with `'x' must be numeric`. The
same input arises in production: a column that is empty in every
row is read by `read.csv()` as logical, and the function then fails
on it. The test has found a real input the function does not
handle, which is what a test is for.
:::

### Exercises

1. `age_group()` is tested for typical ages, boundaries, `NA`, and
   non-numeric input. One gap remains: what the function does with
   an age outside the range the breaks cover. Find the behavior,
   decide whether it is the behavior you want, and write the test
   that pins whichever answer you choose.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-20-1
as.character(age_group(c(-5, 0, 200)))
```

A negative age returns `NA`, because the breaks begin at 0 and
`cut()` places anything below the first break outside every
interval. An age of 200 is absorbed into `65+`, because the last
break is `Inf`. The asymmetry is the finding: an impossible age at
the top of the range is silently accepted, and an impossible age
at the bottom becomes the same `NA` a genuinely missing age
produces. Pinning the current behavior:

```{r}
#| label: soln-20-1b
expect_true(is.na(age_group(-5)),
            info = "age below the first break gives NA")
```

Preferring an error instead, the test comes first and the function
changes to satisfy it:

```{r}
#| label: soln-20-1c
age_group_strict <- function(age) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(age))
  if (any(age < 0, na.rm = TRUE))
    stop("negative age")
  cut(age, breaks = c(0, 18, 40, 65, Inf), right = FALSE,
      labels = c("under-18", "18-39", "40-64", "65+"))
}

expect_error(age_group_strict(-5), pattern = "negative age",
             info = "negative age is rejected")
expect_equal(as.character(age_group_strict(30)), "18-39",
             info = "a valid age still bins correctly")
```

Either is defensible. Leaving the behavior untested is not,
because then it is not a decision at all, only whatever `cut()`
happened to do.
:::

## Structure versus correctness {#sec-testing-correctness}

A test that the result 'is a tibble of the right shape' is a
structural check, not a test of correctness. A test that a
regression coefficient on a known synthetic dataset equals the
closed-form answer, or that a cell survives the pipeline unchanged,
is a test of correctness. Write both, and do not mistake the first
for the second.

### Integration tests on synthetic data

Unit tests catch helper bugs. They do not catch bugs where the
helpers work individually and their composition fails. An
integration test runs the whole pipeline on a small synthetic
dataset:

```{r}
#| label: test-integration
#| message: false
# inst/tinytest/test-pipeline.R
# In a package the test file would load run_pipeline from R/; it is
# defined here so the example executes as written.
run_pipeline <- function(raw) {
  raw |>
    janitor::clean_names() |>
    dplyr::filter(age >= 18) |>
    dplyr::mutate(age_group = age_group(age)) |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(dplyr::starts_with("bp_"),
                        names_to = "visit", names_prefix = "bp_v",
                        values_to = "bp") |>
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(bp)) |>
    dplyr::mutate(visit = as.integer(visit)) |>
    dplyr::select(patient_id, age_group, sex, treatment, visit, bp)
}

# synthetic data that exercises every branch
raw <- tibble::tibble(
  patient_id = c(1, 2, 3, 4),
  age        = c(25, 50, 75, 17),     # one excluded
  bp_v1      = c(120, 140, 160, NA),
  bp_v2      = c(118, 138, NA,  NA),
  sex        = c("M", "F", "F", "M"),
  treatment  = c("placebo", "active", "placebo", "active")
)

clean <- run_pipeline(raw)

expect_inherits(clean, "tbl_df", info = "returns a tibble")
expect_equal(names(clean),
             c("patient_id", "age_group", "sex",
               "treatment", "visit", "bp"),
             info = "column names and order are as specified")

# row count: 3 adults x 2 visits, minus NAs
expect_equal(nrow(clean), 5,
             info = "patient 4 excluded; patient 3 has one NA bp")

expect_equal(clean$bp[clean$patient_id == 1 & clean$visit == 1],
             120,
             info = "a known cell survives the pipeline unchanged")
```

The dataset has four patients and two visits, but it exercises
each cleaning rule: the age exclusion (patient 4) and a missing
value (patient 3, visit 2). The rule generalizes: for each filter,
derivation, pivot, and recode, the fixture has at least one row
that exercises it, including the branches you do not think exist.

### Reference tests

For an output that is tedious to assert literally, compare it with
a stored reference. The first run writes the object to a file and
passes; later runs compare against it.

```{r}
#| label: test-reference
ref_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "lm-coefs.rds")
unlink(ref_file)
fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)

refit <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars[-1, ])

c(first_run = expect_equal_to_reference(coef(fit), ref_file),
  later_run = expect_equal_to_reference(coef(fit), ref_file),
  changed   = expect_equal_to_reference(coef(refit), ref_file))
```

When a reference test fails, you decide whether the change is
intended (delete the file and regenerate it) or a regression. The
stored object is compared by value, so a coefficient that changed
fails and a `print` method that gained a blank line does not.
Inspect the reference once when it is first written, because the
first run accepts whatever the code produced.

| Use a reference test when | Avoid it when |
|---|---|
| The output is complex and tedious to assert literally | The output changes for trivial reasons: an unseeded random draw, the locale, an unstable sort |
| The question is 'is this what was reviewed' | The stored object is too large to inspect when it changes, so 'accept or investigate' becomes a coin toss |

: When a reference test helps. {#tbl-testing-reference}

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Your test asserts `expect_equal(nrow(result), 100)`,
and it passes. Does this mean the result is correct?

**Answer.** No. It says nothing about which rows, what values, or
whether the right rows were filtered; 100 rows of the wrong
patients pass. Add assertions on content:

```{r}
#| label: test-structural-vs-correct
result        <- data.frame(patient_id = 1:100, age = rep(40:49, 10))
expected_ids  <- 1:100
expected_ages <- rep(40:49, 10)

expect_equal(nrow(result), 100)            # structural
expect_equal(sort(result$patient_id),      # correctness
             sort(expected_ids))
expect_equal(result$age, expected_ages)
```

'Looks right at the surface, wrong underneath' is the most common
testing failure in data analysis, and a structural test alone is
built to miss it.
:::

### Exercises

2. Write a `summarize_species()` function returning mean body mass
   and count per species from `palmerpenguins::penguins`. Give it
   one structural test and one correctness test, and say in a
   comment which is which and why the structural one is
   insufficient on its own.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-20-2
#| message: false
library(palmerpenguins)

summarize_species <- function(data) {
  data |>
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(body_mass_g)) |>
    dplyr::group_by(species) |>
    dplyr::summarize(mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g),
                     n = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop")
}

# STRUCTURAL: shape only. Every line below passes even if
# mean_mass is computed as a median, a sum, or the wrong column.
out <- summarize_species(penguins)
expect_inherits(out, "tbl_df", info = "structural: a tibble")
expect_equal(names(out), c("species", "mean_mass", "n"),
             info = "structural: column names")
expect_equal(nrow(out), 3, info = "structural: one row per species")

# CORRECTNESS: values the test computes independently.
adelie <- penguins$body_mass_g[penguins$species == "Adelie"]
expect_equal(out$mean_mass[out$species == "Adelie"],
             mean(adelie, na.rm = TRUE),
             info = "correctness: the mean is the mean")
expect_equal(out$n[out$species == "Adelie"],
             sum(!is.na(adelie)),
             info = "correctness: n counts non-missing")
```

The structural test is worth keeping, because a change in column
names breaks callers. It is insufficient because every assertion
in it would still pass if `mean()` were replaced by `median()`.
Only the second test would fail, and only because it recomputes
the answer a different way rather than comparing the function with
itself.
:::

## Declarative data validation {#sec-testing-declarative}

Every assertion so far is a line of code: `stopifnot()`,
`expect_equal()`, a comparison written against a value you worked
out by hand or derived independently. That style fits a function
with a handful of expected outputs. It fits less well a different
kind of claim, common in a data-cleaning pipeline, that is really
about an entire column at once: every `arm` value is one of two
strings, every `visit_day` is non-negative, every `patient_id` is
unique. Writing each of these as a hand-rolled loop over rows is
possible and unpleasant to read; the loop obscures the rule inside
the machinery that checks it, and a failure reports only that
*something* was wrong, not which rows or how many.

A declarative validation package turns the rule itself into the
unit you write and read. `pointblank` [@iannone2026pointblank] is
the package this section uses; `validate` is a close alternative
with a more compact rule syntax, shown at the end, and either is a
reasonable choice for a project that does not already use the
other. Both are NOT installed in this environment, so every chunk
below is display-only.

### An agent of checks

`pointblank`'s central object is a validation *agent*: you attach a
table, add one validation step per rule, and `interrogate()` the
whole set in one call, producing a report of which rows passed each
rule and which did not. On HF-HOME's randomization table, the
rule that `arm` holds only the two protocol values, and the rule
that `patient_id` is unique within it:

```r
library(pointblank)

rand_agent <- create_agent(tbl = hf_rand, label = "randomization.csv") |>
  col_vals_in_set(columns = arm,
                  set = c("Usual care", "Home health")) |>
  rows_distinct(columns = "patient_id") |>
  interrogate()

rand_agent
all_passed(rand_agent)
```

`col_vals_in_set()` asserts that every value in the column belongs
to the stated set; it does not by itself assert that both values of
a two-level factor actually occur, so a column that happened to
contain only `"Usual care"` would still pass. Where the number of
distinct values matters, not only their membership, pair the agent
with a plain count, the same habit @sec-testing-correctness teaches
for structural versus correctness checks:

```r
stopifnot(length(unique(hf_rand$arm)) == 2)
```

A second agent on the visits table asserts that no contact is
recorded before the index discharge, the rule a negative
`visit_day` would violate:

```r
visits_agent <- create_agent(tbl = hf_visits, label = "visits.csv") |>
  col_vals_gte(columns = visit_day, value = 0) |>
  col_vals_not_null(columns = c(patient_id, visit_type)) |>
  interrogate()

visits_agent
```

Each validation step is readable on its own, independent of the
others, and independent of how the table was produced; that
independence is what a hand-written loop checking several rules at
once loses. `get_agent_report(visits_agent)` returns the per-step
pass and fail counts as a data frame, which is what you want when a
step fails and the next question is 'how many rows, and which
ones', not only 'did it pass'.

### Severity, not just pass or fail

A validation step can be more than a binary gate. `action_levels()`
sets thresholds, for example warn at any failure but stop the
pipeline only once failures exceed a fraction of the rows, which
matches the way a real data-cleaning pipeline tolerates a handful of
exceptions it will route to manual review while still refusing to
proceed on wholesale corruption:

```r
al <- action_levels(warn_at = 1, stop_at = 0.05)

create_agent(tbl = hf_visits, actions = al) |>
  col_vals_gte(columns = visit_day, value = 0) |>
  interrogate()
```

This is the same idea CI applies at the level of a whole test suite
(@sec-ci): a check that can only ever pass completely or fail
completely either blocks every minor exception or hides every major
one, and a graded response lets the two be treated differently
without turning the check off.

### Where a validation agent belongs in a pipeline

A `pointblank` or `validate` check is not a replacement for the
`tinytest` suite; it answers a different question at a different
point in the pipeline. A unit test asserts that a function, given
known input, returns a known output; it runs once, in CI, against
fixtures you wrote. A validation agent asserts that *the data in
hand*, on today's run, satisfies the rules the downstream code
assumes; it belongs inside the cleaning script itself, run every
time the script runs, against whatever extract arrived that day.
Placed right after a raw file is read and before anything
downstream depends on its shape, it catches the HF-HOME equivalent
of @sec-testing-why's opening story, a column whose coding changed
upstream, at the earliest possible point rather than three
transformations later where the error is harder to trace back.

Failing loudly matters here exactly as it does for a test suite's
exit status (@sec-testing-ci): an agent that reports failures but
lets the script continue is a check nobody reads until something
downstream breaks anyway.

```r
rand_agent <- create_agent(tbl = hf_rand) |>
  col_vals_in_set(columns = arm,
                  set = c("Usual care", "Home health")) |>
  rows_distinct(columns = "patient_id") |>
  interrogate()

stopifnot(all_passed(rand_agent))
```

Wrapped in `stopifnot()`, a failed validation step stops the script
exactly as a failed `expect_equal()` stops a test file, and the
same `quit(status = ...)` pattern @sec-testing-ci teaches for a
test suite turns a failed interrogation into a red CI run rather
than a silently truncated dataset three steps downstream. The two
checks are complementary rather than redundant: the unit tests
prove the cleaning function is correct on the cases you anticipated,
and the validation agent proves that today's input still matches
the assumptions those tests were written against.

### `validate`, in brief

`validate`'s rules read like a vector of ordinary R expressions,
which some readers find more directly portable from existing
`stopifnot()` code:

```r
library(validate)

rules <- validator(
  arm %in% c("Usual care", "Home health"),
  visit_day >= 0,
  is_unique(patient_id)
)
out <- confront(hf_rand, rules)
summary(out)
```

`confront()` returns one logical result per rule per row, and
`summary()` collapses that into the pass and fail counts
`pointblank`'s report gives directly. Choose one package for a
project rather than mixing both, for the same reason @sec-testing-unit
gives for choosing one test framework: the discipline is identical
under either, and switching costs more than either tool saves.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A `pointblank` agent reports that `col_vals_gte(columns
= visit_day, value = 0)` passed on 6,317 rows. A colleague says this
proves every visit in the file occurred on or after discharge. Is
that the full claim the check supports?

**Answer.** Close, but the check is about the file as loaded, not
about the file's provenance. It proves that no `visit_day` value in
this snapshot of `visits.csv` is negative; it says nothing about
whether `visit_day` was computed correctly from `visit_date` and
`discharge_date` in the first place, which a value could get wrong
in a way that is still non-negative (an off-by-one day, for
example). A declarative check and a comparison with an
independently derived value answer different questions, and a
pipeline typically needs both, the same lesson
@sec-testing-correctness draws for hand-written assertions.
:::

### Exercises

1. Write the `pointblank` agent (or the `validate` rule set) that
   asserts, on HF-HOME's `outcomes.csv`: `event_30d` is `0`, `1`, or
   missing; `ascertained` is logical with no missing values; and
   `patient_id` is unique. Say which of the three rules a
   hand-written `stopifnot()` would express about as concisely, and
   which one is more naturally a declarative rule.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```r
library(pointblank)

outcomes_agent <- create_agent(tbl = hf_outcomes,
                               label = "outcomes.csv") |>
  col_vals_in_set(columns = event_30d, set = c(0, 1),
                  na_pass = TRUE) |>
  col_vals_not_null(columns = ascertained) |>
  rows_distinct(columns = "patient_id") |>
  interrogate()
outcomes_agent
```

The equivalent with `stopifnot()`:

```r
stopifnot(
  all(hf_outcomes$event_30d %in% c(0, 1, NA)),
  !anyNA(hf_outcomes$ascertained),
  !anyDuplicated(hf_outcomes$patient_id)
)
```

For a fixed, small set of rules run once, the two are about equally
concise; `stopifnot()` wins slightly on `ascertained`, a single
`anyNA()` call. The uniqueness rule is where the declarative version
pulls ahead: `rows_distinct()` names the intent directly, and its
report, unlike `anyDuplicated()`'s single index, lists every
duplicated value when the check fails, which is what you want on
the day it does.
:::

## Test smells {#sec-testing-smells}

Some tests look like tests and produce only confidence. Two run
below; @tbl-testing-smells lists the common kinds.

```{r}
#| label: test-antipattern-tautology
# foo ignores its argument and always returns 42. It is wrong for
# every input, and the test below still passes.
foo <- function(x) 42

expect_equal(foo(1), foo(1),      # always passes
             info = "foo works")
```

```{r}
#| label: test-antipattern-tolerance
result <- 0.9                                # nowhere near 0.5

expect_equal(result, 0.5, tolerance = 0.5)   # passes for 0 to 1
```

The tolerance example passes for any value from 0 to 1. With an
expected value no larger than the tolerance, `all.equal()`, which
`expect_equal()` uses, compares the absolute difference, so a
tolerance of 0.5 around 0.5 accepts every proportion there is.

| Smell | Example | Why it misleads | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tautology | `expect_equal(foo(1), foo(1))` | Compares the function with itself | Compare with a value computed another way |
| Mocking the code under test | A stub `fit_model <- function(d) list()` inside the test | Tests the stub, not the function | Test the real function on a small input |
| Brittle reference | `expect_equal_to_reference(do_thing(Sys.Date()), ...)` | Fails every day after the first, so failures stop being read | Remove the date, or compare stable fields |
| Permissive tolerance | `expect_equal(x, 0.5, tolerance = 0.5)` | Accepts any proportion | Set the tolerance from the computation's real precision |
| Placeholder | `expect_true(TRUE)` | Tests nothing | Write the test or delete the line |
| Prefixed expectation | `tinytest::expect_equal(x, y)` in a test file | Not collected: the file reports zero tests, with only a message | Call `expect_equal()` without the prefix |
| Shape only | `expect_equal(nrow(out), 100)` | Passes on the wrong rows | Assert values (@sec-testing-correctness) |

: Test smells. Watch for them in code review. {#tbl-testing-smells}

`tinytest` has no mocking facility, which makes the second smell
harder to write by accident than under `testthat`'s
`with_mocked_bindings()`.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A colleague's test is
`expect_equal(risk_difference(d), risk_difference(d), tolerance = 1e-8)`.
They point out that the tolerance is tight. Is the test any good?

**Answer.** No. It is a tautology with a tight tolerance: the
expected value comes from calling the function under test, so it
passes whatever the function returns. The tolerance is irrelevant.
The fix is an expected value computed another way, for example
the difference of two proportions worked out by hand on a
ten-row fixture.
:::

### Exercises

3. Replace the tautological test, `expect_equal(foo(1), foo(1))`,
   with an assertion that fails against `foo <- function(x) 42`
   while passing against a correct implementation that doubles its
   argument.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-20-3
#| error: true
foo <- function(x) 42          # wrong for every input

expect_equal(foo(1), 2, info = "foo doubles 1")
expect_equal(foo(3), 6, info = "foo doubles 3")
```

The fix is to assert against a value computed independently of the
function, here by hand. Any assertion whose expected value comes
from calling the function is circular, and no number of added cases
repairs that.
:::

## Style and lint checks {#sec-testing-style}

A test suite checks what code does. Style and lint checks catch a
different kind of problem: code that runs correctly but is hard
enough to read that the next check, a person's own review of the
diff, is weaker than it should be. @sec-ai-coding makes the point
that a diff you cannot read is a diff you cannot audit, which
matters more now that a coding agent can produce a diff faster than
anyone reads one; this section is the mechanics behind that point.
Both tools below are NOT installed in this environment, so the
chunks are display-only.

### `styler` and `lintr`

The `tidyverse` style guide [@wickham2023style] is the de facto
standard in applied R, and two tools apply it:

```r
styler::style_file("R/clean.R")
styler::style_dir("R")

lintr::lint("R/clean.R")
lintr::lint_dir("R")
```

`styler` rewrites whitespace, indentation, and assignment to a
canonical form, so that the diff a reviewer reads shows what
changed rather than whose keyboard it came from. `lintr` is a
static analyzer that flags what `styler` cannot fix, including some
genuine bugs:

```r
lintr::lint(text = "m <- mean(x, na.rm = T)\n",
            linters = lintr::T_and_F_symbol_linter())
```

Run over generated code, `lintr` catches a useful fraction of the
mechanical mistakes in @tbl-ai-failures before you spend attention
on the substantive ones; `T` for `TRUE` is exactly the kind of
planted bug a linter is built to flag.

### `Air`, a faster formatter

`Air` [@vaughan2026air] is a newer, Rust-based formatter and
language server for R from Posit, built for speed: it formats a
file in milliseconds rather than the fraction of a second `styler`
needs, which matters most as a save-on-type action in an editor
rather than as a batch job. As of this writing `Air` is in beta,
and its formatting choices and command-line interface can still
change between releases; check the project's own documentation
before adopting it on a project you cannot easily re-format later.
`usethis::use_air()` wires a project to format with `Air` on save in
supporting editors (RStudio, Positron, VS Code) and from the command
line (display-only):

```r
usethis::use_air()
```

```bash
air format R/
```

`Air` and `styler` are not required to agree on every formatting
choice, so pick one as the project's formatter rather than running
both and reconciling the diffs; `lintr`'s checks are independent of
either and are worth keeping regardless of which formatter you use.

### Automating the check with pre-commit

A style or lint check that someone has to remember to run is a
check that eventually does not run, the same argument
@sec-testing-ci makes for tests. The `precommit` package wires
`styler`, `lintr`, and other R checks into
[pre-commit](https://pre-commit.com), a language-agnostic framework
that runs configured hooks on every `git commit` and refuses the
commit if a hook fails or rewrites a file. A minimal configuration
for an R project (display-only; `precommit` and `pre-commit` are
not installed here):

```yaml
# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/lorenzwalthert/precommit
    rev: v0.4.3
    hooks:
      - id: style-files
      - id: lintr
```

```r
precommit::use_precommit()
```

`use_precommit()` writes the configuration above and installs the
git hook that runs it. Check the `precommit` package's current hook
list for whether it has added an `Air` hook by the time you read
this; if not, a hook that simply shells out to `air format` belongs
in the same file. Either way, the effect is the same one CI gives
the test suite: the check happens on every commit, not only on the
commits where someone remembered to run it by hand, and a commit
that fails the hook never reaches the history for a reviewer to
read in its unformatted form.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A pull request shows a 400-line diff, and the author
says most of it is `styler` reformatting unrelated to the actual
change. How does a reviewer verify that, and why does it matter?

**Answer.** Run `styler::style_file()` (or `air format`) on the
pre-change version of the file and diff that against the
post-change version; what remains is the substantive change.
Without a pre-commit hook, exactly this situation recurs on every
pull request that touches a file nobody has run the formatter on
yet, and a reviewer who skips the check because the diff 'looks
like formatting' is trusting the author's unverified claim about
their own diff, the same shortcut @sec-ai-governance warns against
for a model's unverified claim about its own code.
:::

### Exercises

4. A teammate's project has `styler` and `lintr` configured but no
   pre-commit hook, and a recurring complaint is that pull requests
   mix substantive changes with reformatting because contributors
   forget to run `styler` before committing. Write the
   `.pre-commit-config.yaml` entries that would prevent this, and
   explain what changes about the pull-request diffs once the hook
   is active.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/lorenzwalthert/precommit
    rev: v0.4.3
    hooks:
      - id: style-files
      - id: lintr
```

Once active, every commit is formatted before it is recorded: a
hook that rewrites a file on a failed check (as `style-files` does)
aborts the commit and leaves the reformatted file staged for the
author to commit again, so a reformatted-and-changed file can never
reach the branch in a single, mixed commit. Pull-request diffs then
show only the lines a contributor meant to change, because every
commit already in the history was formatted at the moment it was
made rather than reformatted wholesale later.
:::

## Worked example: testing the HF-HOME CRF cleaner {#sec-testing-worked}

The HF-HOME CRF (case report form) export,
`analysis/data/raw_data/hfhome/crf_export.csv`, comes from five
site systems that each write the same fields differently: Site D
codes sex as `1` and `2`, Site C writes dates month first, Site E
has lost the leading zeros of its patient IDs, and the site labels
vary in case and spacing. The function below puts four fields into
canonical form. Each site's coding lives in a lookup table passed
as an argument with a default, so that the codebook is in one place
and a change to it is a one-line change.

```{r}
#| label: test-crf-fn
#' Clean the site-specific fields of the HF-HOME CRF export
#'
#' @param raw Data frame read from `crf_export.csv`, every column
#'   character.
#' @param site_d_sex Codes Site D uses for sex.
#' @param date_formats Discharge-date format for each site.
#' @return A data frame of `patient_id`, `site`, `sex`, and
#'   `discharge_date` in canonical form.
clean_crf <- function(raw,
                      site_d_sex = c("1" = "M", "2" = "F"),
                      date_formats = c("Site A" = "%Y-%m-%d",
                                       "Site B" = "%Y-%m-%d",
                                       "Site C" = "%m/%d/%Y",
                                       "Site D" = "%d-%b-%Y",
                                       "Site E" = "%Y%m%d")) {
  site <- paste("Site", toupper(substring(trimws(raw$site), 6)))
  sex <- ifelse(site == "Site D", site_d_sex[raw$sex],
                toupper(substr(raw$sex, 1, 1)))
  if (!all(sex %in% c("F", "M"))) {
    stop("unrecognized sex code: ",
         paste(unique(raw$sex[!sex %in% c("F", "M")]),
               collapse = ", "))
  }
  data.frame(
    patient_id     = sprintf("%04d", as.integer(raw$patient_id)),
    site           = site,
    sex            = unname(sex),
    discharge_date = as.Date(raw$discharge_date,
                             format = date_formats[site])
  )
}
```

The test file has two layers. The unit layer is a fixture with one
row per site, each written the way that site writes it, and
expected values worked out by hand from the codebook. The
integration layer cleans the whole export and compares it with two
independent records of the same patients: sex in the registration
demographics and the discharge date in the baseline table.
Agreement between independent sources is a check real trials run,
and it needs no hand-written expectations.[^locale]

[^locale]: `%b` matches English month abbreviations only in an
    English locale. On a machine whose `LC_TIME` is set otherwise,
    Site D's dates parse to `NA`, and the date tests below report
    it.

```{r}
#| label: test-crf-tests
#| eval: false
# inst/tinytest/test-clean-crf.R
hf_dir <- Sys.getenv("HFHOME_DIR")

fixture <- data.frame(
  patient_id     = c("0005", "0001", "0012", "0010", "7"),
  site           = c("Site A", "site b", "SITE C", " Site D", "Site E "),
  sex            = c("F", "Male", "f", "2", "M"),
  discharge_date = c("2024-02-02", "2024-02-01", "02/03/2024",
                     "05-FEB-2024", "20240209")
)
out <- clean_crf(fixture)

expect_equal(out$patient_id, c("0005", "0001", "0012", "0010", "0007"),
             info = "Site E IDs regain their leading zeros")
expect_equal(out$site, paste("Site", LETTERS[1:5]),
             info = "site labels are normalized")
expect_equal(out$sex, c("F", "M", "F", "F", "M"),
             info = "every site's sex coding; Site D codes 2 as F")
expect_equal(out$discharge_date,
             as.Date(c("2024-02-02", "2024-02-01", "2024-02-03",
                       "2024-02-05", "2024-02-09")),
             info = "every site's date format; Site C is month first")
expect_error(clean_crf(transform(fixture, sex = "X")),
             pattern = "unrecognized sex code",
             info = "an unknown sex code stops the cleaning")

crf <- read.csv(file.path(hf_dir, "crf_export.csv"),
                colClasses = "character", fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM")
demographics <- read.csv(file.path(hf_dir, "demographics.csv"),
                         colClasses = "character")
baseline <- read.csv(file.path(hf_dir, "baseline.csv"),
                     colClasses = "character")
both <- merge(clean_crf(crf), demographics[c("patient_id", "sex")],
              by = "patient_id", suffixes = c("", "_demo"))
both <- merge(both, baseline[c("patient_id", "discharge_date")],
              by = "patient_id", suffixes = c("", "_base"))

expect_equal(nrow(both), nrow(crf),
             info = "every CRF patient is found in both sources")
expect_equal(both$sex, both$sex_demo,
             info = "sex agrees with the registration record")
expect_equal(both$discharge_date, as.Date(both$discharge_date_base),
             info = "discharge date agrees with the baseline table")
```

In a project this chunk is the file `inst/tinytest/test-clean-crf.R`.
The chunk below writes it to a temporary file and runs it as
`tinytest` would, with the data directory passed in an environment
variable rather than written into the test.

```{r}
#| label: test-crf-run
test_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "test-clean-crf.R")
writeLines(knitr::knit_code$get("test-crf-tests"), test_file)
hf_env <- list(
  HFHOME_DIR = normalizePath(file.path("..", "data", "raw_data",
                                       "hfhome"))
)

passing <- run_test_file(test_file, verbose = 0, set_env = hf_env)
passing
```

Every test passes. That shows the tests agree with the function;
it does not yet show that they would notice if the function were
wrong. To find out, plant a bug a reviewer could plausibly miss,
here Site D's sex codes swapped, and run the same tests again:

```{r}
#| label: test-crf-mutant
clean_crf_correct <- clean_crf
clean_crf <- function(raw) {
  clean_crf_correct(raw, site_d_sex = c("1" = "F", "2" = "M"))
}

mutant <- run_test_file(test_file, verbose = 0, set_env = hf_env)
mutant

clean_crf <- clean_crf_correct
```

Both layers catch it: the fixture's Site D row, and the comparison
with the registration record, which disagrees for every Site D
patient. The swapped function returns a plausible data frame, with
two sexes in plausible proportions, which is exactly the kind of
bug that survives inspection (Habit 8).

This check has a name: [**mutation testing**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-mutation-testing)
[@demillo1978hints]. Each planted bug is a *mutant*; a test that
fails on it *kills* it; and the share of mutants killed measures
how much the suite can see. Tools for other languages generate
mutants automatically (flipped comparisons, swapped constants,
deleted lines). By hand, plant one mutant per rule in the codebook,
starting with the rules whose failure would produce a plausible
number.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Confirm in code that the suite passes the correct function and
fails the mutant, so that a later edit to the tests cannot quietly
make them blind to it.

```{r}
#| label: test-crf-verify
stopifnot(tinytest::all_pass(passing), tinytest::any_fail(mutant))
```

The chunk prints nothing when both hold.
:::

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
An agentic version: a coding agent writes tests and runs mutants,
and you review the evidence rather than only the code.

> **Context.** `R/clean_crf.R` cleans the HF-HOME CRF export. The
> codebook, `analysis/data/raw_data/hfhome/README.md`, lists each
> site's coding of sex, dates, IDs, and site labels. Existing tests
> are in `inst/tinytest/`. Run code only against the synthetic
> HF-HOME files.
>
> **Constraints.** Add tests in a new file,
> `inst/tinytest/test-clean-crf-sites.R`. Do not edit
> `R/clean_crf.R` or any existing test file, do not skip, delete,
> or loosen a test, and add no packages. If a test you write fails
> against the current function, stop and report it; do not change
> the test to make it pass.
>
> **Criteria.** Before writing tests, list each codebook rule and
> the fixture row that will exercise it. Then, for each rule,
> create one mutant of `clean_crf()` in a temporary copy, run the
> suite against it, and report a table of mutant, killed or
> survived, and the test that killed it.

*Failure mode.* An agent told to make tests pass will weaken them:
it widens a tolerance, replaces a value check with a shape check,
or edits the expected value to match the output. That is why the
instruction forbids touching existing tests, and why the rule that
tests are off-limits to an agent is part of the book's governance
rules (@sec-ai-governance). *Check.* Run
`git diff --stat -- inst/tinytest/ R/` and confirm that only the
new test file changed; read every `expect_*()` in it for a
hand-derived expected value; then run one mutant yourself, as in
the chunk above, and confirm that the suite fails. The codebook
and synthetic files hold no patient data.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Why does the fixture have one row per site, written
by hand, rather than five rows sampled from the export?

**Answer.** Every pathology in the export is per site, so a test
must exercise every site to exercise every branch. Five sampled
rows can easily miss Site D, whose numeric sex codes are the branch
most likely to be wrong, and a sample changes when the export
does. A hand-built row per site exercises each branch on purpose,
and its expected values come from the codebook rather than from the
function.
:::

### Exercises

4. Make a second mutant that parses Site C's dates day first
   (`"%d/%m/%Y"`). Predict which tests kill it, run the suite, and
   count how many Site C dates the mutant gets silently wrong,
   rather than `NA`.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-20-4
day_first <- eval(formals(clean_crf_correct)$date_formats)
day_first["Site C"] <- "%d/%m/%Y"
clean_crf <- function(raw) {
  clean_crf_correct(raw, date_formats = day_first)
}
mutant_c <- run_test_file(test_file, verbose = 0, set_env = hf_env)
mutant_c

crf <- read.csv(file.path(hf_env$HFHOME_DIR, "crf_export.csv"),
                colClasses = "character", fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM")
right <- clean_crf_correct(crf)
wrong <- clean_crf(crf)
in_c <- right$site == "Site C"
c(site_c = sum(in_c),
  became_na = sum(is.na(wrong$discharge_date[in_c])),
  silently_wrong = sum(!is.na(wrong$discharge_date[in_c]) &
                         wrong$discharge_date[in_c] !=
                           right$discharge_date[in_c]))
clean_crf <- clean_crf_correct
```

The fixture's date test and the comparison with the baseline table
both kill the mutant. The counts show why the comparison matters
more than it seems: dates whose day is above 12 become `NA`, which
is loud, but every date whose day is 12 or below, and differs from
its month, parses to a valid date in the wrong month. The third
count is the one that matters: those dates pass every check except
a comparison with something independent.
:::

5. The CRF's `sbp_discharge` column marks a missing value three
   ways: an empty field, `NA`, and `-99`. Write `clean_sbp()`,
   which returns numeric systolic blood pressure with every missing
   code as `NA`, and a test that compares it with
   `sbp_discharge` in `baseline.csv`.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-20-5
clean_sbp <- function(x) {
  x <- trimws(x)
  x[x %in% c("", "NA", "-99")] <- NA
  as.numeric(x)
}

crf_raw <- read.csv(file.path(hf_env$HFHOME_DIR, "crf_export.csv"),
                    colClasses = "character",
                    fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM",
                    na.strings = character())
crf_raw$patient_id <- sprintf("%04d", as.integer(crf_raw$patient_id))
baseline <- read.csv(file.path(hf_env$HFHOME_DIR, "baseline.csv"),
                     colClasses = c(patient_id = "character"))
both <- merge(crf_raw[c("patient_id", "sbp_discharge")],
              baseline[c("patient_id", "sbp_discharge")],
              by = "patient_id", suffixes = c("_crf", "_base"))

expect_equal(clean_sbp(both$sbp_discharge_crf),
             as.numeric(both$sbp_discharge_base),
             info = "every missing code becomes NA; values unchanged")
c(missing_crf = sum(is.na(clean_sbp(both$sbp_discharge_crf))),
  missing_baseline = sum(is.na(both$sbp_discharge_base)))
```

`na.strings = character()` keeps the raw codes as text, so that the
function, not `read.csv()`, decides what is missing; with the
default, `NA` is converted on reading and `-99` is not, and the
test would no longer exercise the function's handling of either. A
version that forgot `-99` would leave impossible pressures of -99
mmHg in the data, which a mean would absorb without complaint; the
comparison with the baseline table fails on it.
:::

## Running tests in continuous integration {#sec-testing-ci}

Tests that run only when someone remembers to run them catch
regressions late. Continuous integration (CI) runs them on every
push. This section sets up the minimal workflow and shows why its
exit status matters; the four sections that follow, from
@sec-ci, cover what a green check proves, how a workflow is
built, how to read a red run, and how to secure the workflow.
For an R package,
`usethis::use_github_action("check-standard")` sets up GitHub
Actions to run `R CMD check`, which runs the tests, on several
operating systems and R versions. For an analysis project, the
equivalent is a workflow that runs the tests. It assumes a
`DESCRIPTION` file listing the project's dependencies, as a
research compendium has; without one, replace `local::.` with the
packages the tests need:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/test.yaml
name: tests

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies@v2
        with:
          packages: |
            local::.
            any::tinytest
      - name: Run tests
        run: |
          Rscript -e 'res <- tinytest::test_all()' \
            -e 'quit(status = as.integer(tinytest::any_fail(res)))'
```

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**A green CI job can contain failing tests.** The second `-e` line
is not optional. `tinytest::test_all()` reports failures but
returns normally, so `Rscript` exits with status 0 and the job
stays green however many tests fail. A CI step fails only on a
nonzero exit status, so the script must turn 'any test failed'
into one.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Run a one-test suite that fails, in a fresh R process as CI would,
with and without the `quit()` line, and compare the exit statuses.

```{r}
#| label: test-ci-exit-status
failing <- file.path(tempdir(), "failing-suite")
dir.create(failing, showWarnings = FALSE)
writeLines("expect_equal(1 + 1, 3)",
           file.path(failing, "test-fail.R"))

r_libs <- paste0("R_LIBS=",
                 paste(.libPaths(), collapse = .Platform$path.sep))
rscript <- function(...) {
  system2(file.path(R.home("bin"), "Rscript"),
          shQuote(c("--vanilla", ...)), env = r_libs,
          stdout = FALSE, stderr = FALSE)
}
run_suite <- sprintf("res <- tinytest::run_test_dir('%s')", failing)

c(without_quit = rscript("-e", run_suite),
  with_quit = rscript("-e", run_suite, "-e",
                      "quit(status = as.integer(tinytest::any_fail(res)))"))
```

Status 0 is what CI reads as success. Only the version with
`quit()` reports the failing test as a failure.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A teammate's workflow runs
`Rscript -e 'tinytest::test_all()'` and has been green for a
month. What do you know about the tests?

**Answer.** Only that the R process started and `test_all()`
returned. Without the `quit(status = ...)` line, a run in which
every test failed also exits with status 0. Open the log of the
latest run and read the summary line, then add the `quit()` line
and push a deliberately failing test to see the job turn red.
:::

## What CI proves {#sec-ci}

You install `janitor` in March to clean column names, the analysis
renders on your laptop, and you never run `renv::snapshot()`. In
June you open a pull request, and a red cross appears beside it.
The log ends with `Error: Process completed with exit code 1.`,
which tells you nothing; a dozen lines above it is the line that
tells you everything, `there is no package called 'janitor'`. Your
laptop remembered the package and the lockfile did not, so without
the red cross a collaborator would have found out at submission.
Continuous integration runs the analysis on a machine that is not
yours, from a clean state, on every push; this section and the
three after it are about making it check what matters and reading
what it reports.

Continuous integration (CI) is the practice of building and
checking a project automatically every time it changes. When you
push a commit, a fresh machine in the cloud checks out the code,
reconstructs the environment, runs the tests, and renders the
report; if anything fails, you are told within minutes. This
chapter uses GitHub Actions, the CI system built into GitHub,
because it is free for public repositories and the R community
maintains ready-made steps for it. Triggers, jobs, and steps on a
clean machine transfer unchanged to GitLab CI and the other
systems.

For a statistician the value is specific. A passing test suite
says the code does what its tests check. A passing CI run says
more: that the analysis reconstructs from `renv.lock` on a machine
that is not yours and produces the report. That second guarantee
is the one that matters when a reviewer, or you in a year, must
rerun the work. The workflow file is boilerplate and can be
copied; what it checks, and therefore what a green check entitles
you to claim, is a decision.

### What a green check is worth

A green check is only as good as what the workflow runs.
@tbl-ci-checklist lists the four things a workflow for an analysis
compendium should establish, in the order the steps run.

| Check | Step | What a pass proves | What it does not prove |
|---|---|---|---|
| The environment restores | `setup-renv` (`renv::restore()`) | Every package in `renv.lock` installs on a clean machine | That the lockfile lists every package the code uses |
| The tests pass | `tinytest`, with an exit status | The statistical checks of @sec-testing-correctness and @sec-testing-worked hold on known inputs | Anything the tests do not assert |
| The report renders | `quarto render` | Every chunk runs from committed files, with no manual step | That the numbers in it are right |
| No secrets in the repository | Review, and the platform's encrypted secrets | Credentials live outside version control | That printed values are masked; see @sec-ci-security |

: The CI checklist for an analysis compendium. A workflow that
restores and renders but does not test proves that the report
compiles, not that it is correct. {#tbl-ci-checklist}

The first row has a gap that the `janitor` story falls into. A
restore installs what the lockfile lists, so a package the
lockfile omits does not fail the restore; it fails the first later
step that loads it. That is why the rows are a stack, not a menu:
the test and render steps are what discover that the restore was
incomplete.

Fail loudly and early. Humble and Farley's advice for software
delivery, 'if it hurts, do it more frequently, and bring the pain
forward' [@humble2010continuous], applies unchanged to research
code. The purpose of CI is to surface a break at
the commit that introduced it, when the cause is one small diff,
rather than at submission, when the cause is buried in months of
history. Every step must fail the job when its check fails, not
warn and continue.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Your workflow restores `renv` and renders the
report, and the check is green. A collaborator reports that a
figure differs from yours. What does the green check tell you, and
what does it not?

**Answer.** It tells you that the analysis reconstructs from
`renv.lock` on a clean machine and that the report renders, so the
discrepancy is not a missing package or an uncommitted file. It
does not tell you the figure is correct, because nothing in the
workflow tests the figure's content. Suspect an unseeded random
step, a different data version, or a genuine analytic difference,
and add a test that pins the figure's underlying numbers so that CI
catches the change next time.
:::

### Exercises

6. A workflow restores `renv.lock`, runs a `tinytest` suite whose
   only test checks that the analytic dataset has the expected
   columns, and renders the report. For each change below, say
   which step turns the run red, or whether the run stays green.
   (a) The code calls `janitor`, which is installed on your laptop
   but absent from the lockfile. (b) A chunk reads
   `data/derived/cohort.rds`, a file listed in `.gitignore`. (c)
   The primary analysis computes a median where the plan specifies
   a mean. (d) Someone pastes an API token into the workflow file.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
(a) Not the restore, which succeeds because it installs only what
the lockfile lists; the run turns red at the first step that loads
`janitor`, the tests if they call it, otherwise the render. (b) The
render: the file exists on your machine and not on the runner. (c)
Nothing; the run stays green, because the only test checks the
shape of the data, not a value (Habit 9). (d) Nothing; the run
stays green, and the token is now in the Git history of a
repository that may be public. Revoke it, then move it to the
platform's encrypted secrets. Two of the four failures pass every
step, which is the point of the last column of @tbl-ci-checklist.
:::

## Anatomy of a workflow {#sec-ci-anatomy}

A GitHub Actions workflow is a YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language)
file in `.github/workflows/`. It names the events that trigger it,
one or more jobs, and the steps within each job. The steps run in
order on a fresh virtual machine, called a runner, that GitHub
provisions for the run. @fig-ci-anatomy is the shape before the
syntax.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-ci-anatomy
%%| fig-alt: "Flowchart of a CI workflow run. A push to main or a
%%|   pull request triggers a fresh virtual machine, which then
%%|   checks out the repository, installs R, runs renv::restore() to
%%|   prove the lockfile is complete, runs the tests to prove the
%%|   numbers are right, and runs quarto render to prove the report
%%|   builds. A decision node asks whether every step exited zero:
%%|   yes gives a green check, no gives a red cross with a log
%%|   naming the failing step."
%%| fig-cap: "The anatomy of a workflow run. The machine is fresh
%%|   every time, which is what makes the result meaningful: the
%%|   analysis is rebuilt from what is in the repository rather than
%%|   from the state of anyone's laptop. Any step that exits
%%|   non-zero fails the run."
flowchart TD
  E["<b>Trigger</b><br/><i>push to main, or<br/>a pull request</i>"]
  E --> M["<b>Fresh virtual machine</b><br/><i>nothing of yours on it</i>"]
  M --> S1["checkout the repository"]
  S1 --> S2["install R"]
  S2 --> S3["renv::restore()<br/><i>proves the lockfile is complete</i>"]
  S3 --> S4["run the tests<br/><i>proves the numbers are right</i>"]
  S4 --> S5["quarto render<br/><i>proves the report builds</i>"]
  S5 --> P{"all steps<br/>exit zero?"}
  P -->|"yes"| G["green check"]
  P -->|"no"| R["red cross,<br/>log names the failing step"]
```

The workflow below implements the checklist (display-only; it runs
on GitHub, not in this book):

```yaml
name: Check analysis

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          use-public-rspm: true

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2

      - uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2

      - name: Run tests
        run: |
          Rscript -e 'res <- tinytest::test_all()' \
            -e 'quit(status = as.integer(tinytest::any_fail(res)))'

      - name: Render report
        run: quarto render
```

Read it top to bottom. The `on` block runs the workflow on every
push to `main` and on every pull request. The single job, `check`,
runs on a fresh Ubuntu runner. Its steps check out the code,
install R, restore the exact package versions in `renv.lock`,
install Quarto, run the test suite, and render the report. If any
step exits with a nonzero status, the job fails and GitHub marks
the commit with a red cross; if every step exits zero, a green
check.

### Three details that decide the result

**The runner has only what the workflow installs.** R is there
because `setup-r` installed it and Quarto because
`quarto-actions/setup` did; drop the Quarto step and the render
fails with 'command not found'.

**The test step must fail on a failed test.** The second `-e`
expression turns 'any test failed' into a nonzero exit status,
which is the only signal CI reads; without it the job stays green
however many tests fail, as the demonstration in @sec-testing-ci
showed.

**Restore the lockfile, not the latest versions.** The
`r-lib/actions` collection supplies two ways to provide packages,
and they are alternatives, not companions:

| Step | Installs | CI then tests |
|---|---|---|
| `setup-renv` | The exact versions recorded in `renv.lock` | The environment you pinned |
| `setup-r-dependencies` | Current versions of the packages a `DESCRIPTION` file names | Whatever CRAN offers today |

The minimal workflow of @sec-testing-ci uses
`setup-r-dependencies`, which suits a package that must work with
current versions. A compendium with a lockfile wants `setup-renv`,
and every package
the tests call, `tinytest` included, must therefore be in the
lockfile.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**`continue-on-error: true` turns a red step green.** The setting
is sometimes added to a test step 'until the tests are fixed'. The
step still fails, but the job is reported as passing, so the
commit gets a green check, branch protection lets the pull request
merge, and nobody opens the log. Remove the setting and fix or
delete the failing test instead.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Before you push, run the two R steps the way CI will, in a fresh
process from the project root (display-only):

```bash
Rscript -e 'renv::status()'
Rscript -e 'res <- tinytest::test_all()' \
  -e 'quit(status = as.integer(tinytest::any_fail(res)))'
echo $?
```

`renv::status()` should report no issues, and the last line should
print 0. With a failing test planted, it should print 1, as in
@sec-testing-ci.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A teammate replaces `setup-renv` with
`setup-r-dependencies` because the restore 'kept failing', and the
run turns green. What has the green check stopped proving?

**Answer.** That the analysis reproduces with the package versions
in `renv.lock`. The run now tests whatever versions CRAN serves
today, so a result that changed because a dependency changed would
pass without notice, which is the silent regression @sec-renv
exists to prevent. Find out why the restore failed (usually a
system library, @sec-ci-reading) and fix that instead.
:::

### Exercises

7. Add a weekly scheduled run, at 06:00 UTC (Coordinated Universal
   Time) every Monday, to the workflow above, and explain what a
   scheduled run catches in a project whose packages are pinned.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
Add a `schedule` trigger to the `on` block:

```yaml
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 6 * * 1'
```

The five fields are minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of
week (1 is Monday), in UTC. A pinned lockfile does not mean
nothing changes: the runner image is updated, archived package
sources move, and an external data source or URL the report reads
can disappear. A weekly run finds these on a quiet Monday rather
than on the day you need to rerun the analysis.
:::

## Reading a failing run {#sec-ci-reading}

When a run fails, GitHub shows the job's log with the failing step
expanded. Read it from the first error, not from the bottom: the
first error is usually the cause, and everything below it is
consequence. The chunk below reproduces the `janitor` story of
@sec-ci. It
builds a two-file test suite in which one file uses `janitor`,
then runs the CI test step in a fresh R process whose library
holds `tinytest` and nothing else, as a runner restored from a
lockfile that omits `janitor` would.

```{r}
#| label: ci-red-log
ci_run <- function(args, libs = NULL) {
  env <- character()
  if (!is.null(libs)) {
    empty <- file.path(tempdir(), "ci-empty-lib")
    dir.create(empty, showWarnings = FALSE)
    env <- c(paste0("R_LIBS=", libs), paste0("R_LIBS_USER=", empty),
             paste0("R_LIBS_SITE=", empty))
  }
  suppressWarnings(system2(file.path(R.home("bin"), "Rscript"),
                           shQuote(c("--vanilla", args)), env = env,
                           stdout = TRUE, stderr = TRUE))
}

proj <- file.path(tempdir(), "ci-demo")
dir.create(file.path(proj, "tests"), recursive = TRUE,
           showWarnings = FALSE)
writeLines("expect_equal(1 + 1, 2)",
           file.path(proj, "tests", "test-arith.R"))
writeLines(c(
  "library(janitor)",
  "raw <- data.frame(`Patient ID` = '0001', check.names = FALSE)",
  "expect_equal(names(clean_names(raw)), 'patient_id')"
), file.path(proj, "tests", "test-clean.R"))

ci_lib <- file.path(tempdir(), "ci-lib")
dir.create(ci_lib, showWarnings = FALSE)
if (!file.exists(file.path(ci_lib, "tinytest"))) {
  file.symlink(find.package("tinytest"), file.path(ci_lib, "tinytest"))
}

red_log <- ci_run(c(
  "-e", sprintf("res <- tinytest::run_test_dir('%s')",
                file.path(proj, "tests")),
  "-e", "quit(status = as.integer(tinytest::any_fail(res)))"
), libs = ci_lib)
cat(sprintf("%2d  %s", seq_along(red_log), red_log), sep = "\n")
```

GitHub then appends one line of its own,
`Error: Process completed with exit code 1.`, marks the step with a
red cross, and skips the render step. @tbl-ci-log annotates the
lines.

| Line | Text begins | What it is | Act on it? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `test-arith.R` | A test file that ran and passed | No |
| 2 | `Error in library(janitor)` | **The first error: the cause** | Yes: the package is not installed on the runner |
| 3 | `Calls:` | The call stack that led to the error | Only to find which file raised it |
| 4 | `Execution halted` | R stopping because of line 2 | No |
| last | `Error: Process completed with exit code 1.` | GitHub's summary of the step | No; it is the same for every failure |

: The red log, line by line. The line people read is the last one,
and it is the only line that is identical for every failure.
{#tbl-ci-log}

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Confirm that the step failed for the reason the log names, by
checking the exit status and extracting the first error line:

```{r}
#| label: ci-red-log-verify
first_error <- grep("^Error", red_log, value = TRUE)[1]
stopifnot(attr(red_log, "status") == 1, grepl("janitor", first_error),
          identical(first_error, red_log[2]))
first_error
```

On a real run, search the log for the first line that begins with
`Error` (or `ERROR`, or `!` for an `rlang` error) in the failing
step, and read up to three lines around it.
:::

### The fix belongs in the lockfile

The cause is that `renv.lock` omits a package the code uses, so the
fix is on your machine: `renv::status()` reports the package as
used but not recorded, `renv::snapshot()` records it, and you
commit the lockfile (@sec-renv-honest). The run turns green
because the environment is now pinned, not because CI was made to
tolerate it.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**Installing the missing package in the workflow makes the run
green and the analysis irreproducible.** A step such as
`Rscript -e 'install.packages("janitor")'` before the tests fixes
the red cross in one line. The runner now has a package the
lockfile does not record, at whatever version CRAN serves that day,
and the green check proves exactly what it was meant to disprove:
that the analysis depends on something outside `renv.lock`. Fix
the lockfile, never the workflow.
:::

### Common failures

| Failing step | First error looks like | Usual cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `setup-renv` | A compiler or `configure` error naming a system library | A package needs a system library the runner lacks | Install it with `apt-get` in a step before `setup-renv` |
| Tests | `there is no package called 'x'` | Package used but not in `renv.lock` | `renv::snapshot()` locally; commit the lockfile |
| Tests | `expect_equal` failure with observed and expected values | A statistical check did not hold | Read both values; find the change that moved them |
| Render | `cannot open the connection`, or `object 'x' not found` | A chunk depends on a file or object made outside the document | Build it in the pipeline, or commit the input if it is raw data |
| Render | `quarto: command not found` | No Quarto setup step | Add `quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup` |

: Reading a red run. {#tbl-ci-failures}

The book you are reading is built this way: its workflow,
`.github/workflows/render-book.yml`, restores its packages,
provisions R and Python when the book needs them, and renders the
whole book on every push and pull request, so that a broken chunk
is caught before it reaches the published site.

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
> **Context.** Below are the failing step of a GitHub Actions log,
> `.github/workflows/check.yml`, and the output of
> `git diff main -- renv.lock` for an R analysis compendium that
> uses `renv` and `tinytest`.
>
> **Constraints.** Do not edit the workflow file, add an install
> step, or change or skip any test. Propose changes only to
> `renv.lock` (through `renv` commands) or to the analysis code.
>
> **Criteria.** Quote the first error line in the log and say which
> step raised it. Name the cause in one sentence and give the
> commands that fix it on my machine. State what `renv::status()`
> and `git diff --stat` should show after the fix.

*Failure mode.* The model proposes the one-line install step of the
Pitfall above, or `continue-on-error: true`, because either makes
the run green. *Check.* After the fix, `git diff --stat` should
list `renv.lock` and nothing under `.github/` or `inst/tinytest/`,
and the next run should be green. Logs are safe to send when they
contain only code, package names, and test messages; a test that
prints data rows puts data in the log (@sec-ai-governance).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A log shows `Error in library(janitor)` on line 2
and twenty more errors below it, each saying an object is not
found. Which do you fix?

**Answer.** Line 2. The later errors are consequences: the objects
were never created because the code that would have created them
needed `janitor`. Fixing them one at a time patches symptoms of a
single cause, and they disappear when the package is in the
lockfile.
:::

### Exercises

8. The chunk below runs the render step of a two-chunk document in
   a fresh process, as CI would. Read the log and identify the
   cause, why the document renders on its author's machine, and
   the fix.

```{r}
#| label: ci-render-log
render_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "ci-render")
dir.create(render_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
writeLines(c(
  "---", "title: Primary analysis", "---", "",
  "```{r}", "#| label: load-cohort",
  "cohort <- readRDS('data/derived/cohort.rds')", "```", "",
  "```{r}", "#| label: primary",
  "mean(cohort$event_30d, na.rm = TRUE)", "```"
), file.path(render_dir, "paper.qmd"))

render_log <- ci_run(c("-e", sprintf(paste0(
  "setwd('%s'); options(cli.unicode = FALSE); ",
  "knitr::opts_chunk$set(error = FALSE); ",
  "knitr::knit('paper.qmd', quiet = TRUE)"), render_dir)))
cat(render_log, sep = "\n")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
The first error, `cannot open the connection`, does not name the
file; the backtrace beneath it does: `readRDS()` could not find
`data/derived/cohort.rds`, in the chunk labeled `load-cohort`.
The file exists on the author's machine because they built it
once, by hand or with a script the document does not run, and it
is a derived file, so it is (correctly) not committed. The fix is
to make the pipeline build it: run the script that writes it in a
step before the render, or have the document call that script, so
that a clean checkout can produce it (Habit 2). Committing the
`.rds` file instead would make the run green while leaving a build
product that nobody can regenerate.

```{r}
#| label: soln-20-8
stopifnot(attr(render_log, "status") == 1,
          any(grepl("cohort.rds", render_log, fixed = TRUE)))
```
:::

9. A run fails in the `setup-renv` step. Two hundred lines into the
   log, the first error reads
   `configure: error: gdal-config not found or not executable.`
   What failed, and what do you change?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
A package that links to GDAL (the Geospatial Data Abstraction
Library), such as `sf`, was being compiled from source, and its
configure script could not find the GDAL development files on the
runner. Nothing is wrong with the lockfile. Add a step before
`setup-renv` that installs the system libraries, for example
`sudo apt-get install -y libgdal-dev libgeos-dev libproj-dev`, or
build in the project's Docker image (@sec-docker), which already
has them. This is the case @sec-renv-docker describes: `renv`
pins R packages, not the system libraries beneath them.
:::

## Securing the workflow {#sec-ci-security}

A workflow file is code that runs with access to your repository
and to any secrets you give it, and it is version-controlled and
often public. Credentials, tokens, and any protected data belong in
the platform's encrypted secrets, never in the workflow file; the
de-identification discipline of @sec-deident applies to the
pipeline as much as to the data. Three further habits come from
software supply-chain security, and each is a few lines of YAML.

**Pin actions by commit, not by tag.** `uses: actions/checkout@v4`
names a tag, and the owner of a repository can move a tag to
different code. In March 2025 the tags of the widely used
`tj-actions/changed-files` action were repointed to a malicious
commit that printed the secrets of the workflows using it into
their run logs.[^tj-actions] A full 40-character commit SHA (secure
hash algorithm identifier) cannot be moved.

**Grant the workflow token the least permission that works.** Each
run receives a `GITHUB_TOKEN` whose default permissions depend on
repository and organization settings. A `permissions:` block at the
top of the workflow sets them explicitly; a workflow that only
reads code and runs checks needs `contents: read`.

**Use OIDC instead of stored cloud keys.** A workflow that uploads
to a cloud bucket should not hold a long-lived access key in its
secrets. With OpenID Connect (OIDC), the run asks the cloud
provider for short-lived credentials for one role, and the
provider trusts only runs from your repository and branch.

| Practice | Risk it removes | YAML |
|---|---|---|
| Pin by SHA | A moved tag runs code you never reviewed | `uses: owner/action@<40-hex SHA> # v4.4.0` |
| Least permission | A compromised step writes to the repository | `permissions:` with `contents: read` |
| OIDC | A leaked long-lived key works until someone revokes it | `id-token: write` and the provider's login action |
| Dependabot | SHA pins go stale and miss security fixes | `.github/dependabot.yml`, ecosystem `github-actions` |
| Secrets, never values | A token in Git history is public forever | `${{ secrets.NAME }}` |

: Supply-chain basics for a workflow. {#tbl-ci-security}

[^tj-actions]: The incident is CVE-2025-30066: tags v1 through
    v45.0.7 pointed at the malicious commit on 14 and 15 March
    2025. The SHA shown for
    `actions/checkout` in the next listing was read from the
    action's repository with `git ls-remote` in October 2026.

The hardened top of the workflow, with one action pinned
(display-only):

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4.4.0
```

The comment keeps the version readable. Pins do not update
themselves, so add a Dependabot configuration that opens a pull
request when a pinned action has a new release, with the SHA and
the comment both updated. Version updates are the safeguard here,
because Dependabot alerts for vulnerable actions cover only
actions referenced by a version tag, not those pinned to a SHA
(display-only):

```yaml
# .github/dependabot.yml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: github-actions
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
```

A job that needs cloud access requests the OIDC token and nothing
else beyond reading the code (display-only; the role and the
provider's trust policy are configured on the cloud side, and the
login step is the provider's action):

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write
```

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
List every action reference in a workflow that is not pinned to a
full commit SHA, and check for a `permissions:` block. The chunk
writes the hardened example to a file and audits it.

```{r}
#| label: ci-audit-pins
audit_workflow <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path)
  uses <- trimws(sub(".*uses:\\s*", "",
                     grep("uses:", lines, value = TRUE)))
  uses <- sub("\\s*#.*$", "", uses)
  list(unpinned = uses[!grepl("@[0-9a-f]{40}$", uses)],
       has_permissions = any(grepl("^permissions:", lines)))
}

hardened <- file.path(tempdir(), "check.yml")
writeLines(c(
  "permissions:", "  contents: read", "jobs:", "  check:",
  "    runs-on: ubuntu-latest", "    steps:",
  paste0("      - uses: actions/checkout@",
         "11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4.4.0")
), hardened)
audit <- audit_workflow(hardened)
stopifnot(length(audit$unpinned) == 0, audit$has_permissions)
audit
```

Run `audit_workflow()` on each file in your `.github/workflows/`;
an empty `unpinned` and `TRUE` are what you want.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Your workflow pins every action to a tag such as
`@v2`, the actions come from well-known organizations, and none of
your secrets has leaked. Why pin by SHA anyway?

**Answer.** Because a tag is a pointer its owner, or anyone who
compromises the owner's account, can move, and your workflow
follows it without a change to your repository. The
`tj-actions` compromise reached many repositories that had never
changed a line. A SHA pin means the code that runs is the code you
pinned, and Dependabot turns each update into a pull request you
review.
:::

### Exercises

10. Audit this book's own workflow,
    `.github/workflows/render-book.yml`, with `audit_workflow()`.
    Then read the file and answer: what triggers it, when does it
    provision R and Python, which step renders the book, and which
    step receives secrets?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-20-10
book_wf <- file.path("..", "..", ".github", "workflows",
                     "render-book.yml")
if (file.exists(book_wf)) audit_workflow(book_wf)
```

At the time of writing every action in the file is pinned by tag,
not SHA, and there is no `permissions:` block; the output above
shows the current state. The workflow runs on a push to `main`, on
a pull request against `main`, and on manual dispatch
(`workflow_dispatch`). If a `Dockerfile` is present it builds the
project's image and renders inside it; otherwise a detection step
searches `analysis/report` and provisions R when any file contains
an `{r}` chunk or a `renv.lock` exists, and Python when any file
contains a `{python}` chunk.
The step named 'Render book (host)' or 'Render book (container)'
runs `quarto render analysis/report --to html`. The deploy step,
which runs only on a push to `main`, is the one that receives the
Netlify secrets, and it is a third-party action: the strongest
case in the file for a SHA pin.
:::

## For testthat readers {#sec-testing-testthat}

`testthat` is the framework you are most likely to meet elsewhere,
and where a project already depends on it, stay with it; mixing
frameworks in one suite buys nothing. The discipline of this
chapter is the same under either, and most of the translation is
mechanical (@tbl-testing-testthat).

| `tinytest` | `testthat` |
|---|---|
| `expect_equal(x, y, info = "...")` at the top level of the file | `test_that("...", { expect_equal(x, y) })` |
| `expect_inherits(x, "tbl_df")` | `expect_s3_class(x, "tbl_df")` |
| `expect_equal(names(x), c(...))` | `expect_named(x, c(...))` |
| `expect_equal(sort(a), sort(b))` | `expect_setequal(a, b)` |
