| `expect_equal_to_reference(x, "ref.rds")`, stores the object | `expect_snapshot()`, stores printed output; `expect_snapshot_value()`, stores the value |
| `tinysnapshot::expect_snapshot_plot(p, "label")` | `vdiffr::expect_doppelganger("label", p)` |
| `run_test_file()`, `test_all()` | `test_file()`, `devtools::test()` |

: The same tests in both frameworks. {#tbl-testing-testthat}

`tinytest`'s missing functions are a choice rather than a gap: each
is a plain comparison whose failure prints the two values. Visual
regression testing of `ggplot2` output is the one place the two
ecosystems differ in maturity. `vdiffr`, which stores an SVG
(Scalable Vector Graphics) file of the plot and compares later
renders with it, runs only inside `testthat`; `tinysnapshot` is the
`tinytest` equivalent, younger and less widely used.


## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 9: test the statistics, not the shape.** Every test
   file needs at least one assertion against a value computed
   another way: by hand, in closed form, or from an independent
   source. A green check is only as good as what it runs: restore,
   test the statistics, and render; a workflow that renders
   without testing proves the report compiles.
2. **Habit 8: plant the bug before you trust the test, and make
   the quiet failure loud.** A suite you have never seen fail has
   not shown that it can; run one mutant per codebook rule. The
   exit status is the only signal CI reads; turn failed tests into
   a nonzero status, and never set `continue-on-error` on a check.
3. **Habit 4: pin the environment, including the CI's own.** Run
   the tests in CI on every push, restore from the lockfile, pin
   actions by SHA, and fix a red restore in `renv.lock`, never with
   an install step in the workflow.

## Cumulative practice

11. *Cumulative (uses @sec-git-teams).* Review a colleague's test
    suite rather than their code. For each test, decide whether it
    checks statistical content or only structure, and find at least
    one test that would pass even if the function under test were
    subtly wrong. Write the mutant that survives, propose the
    value-level assertion that kills it, and deliver the review as a
    pull-request comment.
12. *Cumulative (uses @sec-renv).* Write the complete workflow for
    the HF-HOME compendium: it runs on pull requests and on pushes
    to `main`, sets `contents: read`, restores `renv.lock`, installs
    Quarto, fails on any failed `tinytest` test, and renders
    `analysis/report`. Add the Dependabot file, and check both
    against @tbl-ci-checklist and @tbl-ci-security.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
12. The workflow:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/check.yml
name: Check analysis

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<sha> # v4.4.0
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@<sha> # v2
        with:
          use-public-rspm: true
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@<sha> # v2
      - uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@<sha> # v2
      - name: Run tests
        run: |
          Rscript -e 'res <- tinytest::test_all()' \
            -e 'quit(status = as.integer(tinytest::any_fail(res)))'
      - name: Render report
        run: quarto render analysis/report
```

Replace each `<sha>` with the commit the tag points to, from
`git ls-remote https://github.com/<owner>/<repo> refs/tags/<tag>`;
for a tag that `git ls-remote` lists twice, use the line ending in
`^{}`, which is the commit. The Dependabot file is the one in
@sec-ci-security. Against the checklist: restore, test, and render
are each a step that fails the job, no secret appears, the token
can only read, and every action is pinned. The workflow needs no
secrets at all, which is the best case.
:::

13. *On your own work (no key).* Add unit tests for two functions
    from an analysis of yours (a typical case, an edge case, and an
    error), an integration test on a synthetic fixture that
    exercises every branch, and a CI workflow that runs them; push
    it and confirm the run is green. Plant one mutant and confirm
    that the suite, and the CI job, turn red. Then remove one
    package from `renv.lock` while leaving its use in the code, push
    to a branch, find the first error in the log, and restore the
    lockfile.

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Code, YAML, or command | Guards against |
|---|---|---|
| Assert a value | `expect_equal(f(x), expected, info = "...")` | A function that returns the wrong number |
| Assert an error | `expect_error(f(bad), pattern = "...")` | Bad input passing silently |
| Assert a class | `expect_inherits(x, "data.frame")` | A changed return type |
| Compare with a stored object | `expect_equal_to_reference(x, "ref.rds")` | Unreviewed changes to complex output |
| Run one file | `run_test_file("test-x.R", set_env = list(...))` | Tests that depend on the working directory |
| Run every test | `tinytest::test_all()` | Untested corners of the project |
| Check the tests can see a bug | Plant a mutant; `any_fail(res)` | A suite that passes everything |
| Run CI on every change | `on: push` and `pull_request` | Breaks found at submission |
| Restore pinned packages | `r-lib/actions/setup-renv` | Testing versions you never used |
| Install Quarto | `quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup` | `quarto: command not found` |
| Fail CI on a failed test | `quit(status = as.integer(tinytest::any_fail(res)))` | A green job with failing tests |
| Run weekly | `schedule: - cron: '0 6 * * 1'` | Drift outside the lockfile |
| Pin an action | `uses: owner/action@<40-hex SHA> # vX` | A moved tag |
| Least permission | `permissions: contents: read` | A step that can write to the repository |
| Short-lived cloud access | `id-token: write` (OIDC) | Long-lived keys in secrets |
| Keep pins current | `.github/dependabot.yml`, `github-actions` | Stale pins |
| Read a red run | First `Error` line in the failing step | Fixing consequences |

: Testing and CI at a glance. {#tbl-testing-cheat-sheet}

## Further reading

- [@wickham2023rpkgs], the testing chapters, the canonical
  `testthat` reference, whose advice on designing a suite applies
  under either framework.
- [@demillo1978hints], the paper that introduced mutation
  analysis as a way to judge test data.
- [@humble2010continuous], *Continuous Delivery*, the book that
  made the argument for continuous integration that this chapter
  applies to research code.

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-20}

1. Even a one-off analysis benefits from tests: they catch
   regressions when you refactor mid-analysis, they serve as
   executable documentation of expected behavior, and they detect
   silent failures when upstream data change format. The cost of
   writing a handful of tests is small; the cost of silently
   mis-analyzing data is much larger.
2. A unit test exercises a single function with known inputs and
   checks the output. An integration test runs a pipeline segment
   (multiple functions) on synthetic data and checks the
   pipeline's output. An end-to-end test runs the full analysis
   pipeline from raw data to final figures and tables. Unit tests
   are fast and narrow; end-to-end tests are slow and broad;
   integration tests sit in between, with good cost-benefit for
   analytic pipelines.
3. Continuous integration automatically builds and checks a
   project on every change: it reconstructs the environment, runs
   the tests, and renders the report. It automates the clean-state
   rerun that a disciplined analyst might do by hand occasionally,
   but does it on every push and on a machine that is not theirs.
   'It renders on my machine' depends on packages, files, and
   manual steps that exist only on your machine and may not be
   recorded. CI reconstructs the analysis from the committed
   sources and `renv.lock` on a clean machine, so a passing run
   demonstrates that the analysis is reproducible from what is
   actually in the repository, not from the state of your laptop.
